html:
Time Series Analysis

This is a reader on time-series econometrics, developed as one line of argument: from dynamic regression and ARMA, through autocorrelation, volatility (ARCH/GARCH), unit roots and forecasting, to multivariate cointegration and VARs, then structural identification of macro shocks (short-run, long-run, external instruments), local projections, and finally maximum likelihood and the Kalman filter for "unobserved states and time-varying coefficients".

Cross-section econometrics assumes the sample is drawn independently from a population; a time series is one path of a stochastic process, observations depend on each other, and time cannot be reversed. Four questions that must be kept apart run through the text:

  1. Forecasting: does the past help predict the future?
  2. Dynamic propagation: once a shock enters the system, how does its effect unfold over horizons?
  3. Causal identification: can the shock be interpreted as exogenous and economically meaningful?
  4. State estimation: after seeing the data, how should we update our view of an unobserved coefficient or state?

A good fit or accurate forecast does not answer question 3, and the Kalman filter does not by itself solve endogeneity. Each chapter first says what question it answers and the intuition, then gives results and derivations, and finally checks them with a worked example.

Prerequisites: linear algebra, basic probability and regression (OLS, t/F tests, the idea of instrumental variables); the Econometrics document in this library helps.

Contents

  1. Overview: What Time-Series Analysis Does
  2. Time-Series Regression and Distributed Lags
  3. OLS with Time Series: Finite-Sample and Large-Sample Theory
  4. Trends, Seasonality and Transformations
  5. AR, MA and ARMA: Dynamic Propagation
  6. ACF, PACF and Box–Jenkins Modelling
  7. Residual Autocorrelation: Tests, Modelling and Robust Inference
  8. Heteroskedasticity, ARCH and GARCH
  9. Unit Roots, Stochastic Trends and DF/ADF Tests
  10. Forecasting, Forecast Errors and Model Comparison
  11. Spurious Regression, Cointegration and Error Correction
  12. VARs: Systems, Estimation and Stability
  13. SVARs: Identification and Impulse Responses
  14. Long-Run Restrictions and Blanchard–Quah Identification
  15. Macro Shocks: Narrative, High-Frequency and External Instruments
  16. Local Projections and LP-IV
  17. Monetary Policy Shocks: Comparing Six Methods

  19. State Space and the Kalman Filter
  20. Time-Varying-Parameter Taylor Rules with GARCH
  21. Review: Choosing Methods and Easily Confused Concepts

Notation

Symbol Meaning
t=1,\ldots,T time and sample length
h forecast or impulse-response horizon; h=0 is the current period
\mathcal I_t information set known at time t
L lag operator, Ly_t=y_{t-1}; \Delta y_t=y_t-y_{t-1}
\varepsilon_t,u_t innovation, disturbance; meaning fixed by the model
\gamma_k,\rho_k autocovariance and autocorrelation at lag k
I(0),I(1) stationary short-memory process; process stationary after one difference
A_i,\Sigma_u lag matrices and innovation covariance of a reduced-form VAR
C,\Theta_h,\Psi_h impact matrix of structural shocks; structural and reduced-form impulse responses
\beta_{t\mid s},P_{t\mid s} conditional mean and error covariance of the state given information up to s

The same letter (B,\Omega,F,\ldots) can denote different objects in different chapters; this text keeps them apart and says so where it matters.

0. Overview: What Time-Series Analysis Does

The text has three connected strands:

Strand Main question Tools
Univariate / single equation How does a series depend on its past? How to forecast? dynamic regression, ARMA, ARCH/GARCH, unit roots
Multivariate and causal shocks How do variables feed back on each other? How do exogenous shocks propagate? cointegration, VAR/SVAR, long-run restrictions, external IV, local projections
Unobserved states How do coefficients or latent states evolve? MLE, state space, Kalman filter, TVP

The modelling workflow is iterative: look at the series (plots, frequency, seasonal adjustment, transformations), judge stationarity, propose dynamics, repair them with residual diagnostics, and finally judge the model by out-of-sample forecasts. Chapters are organised by tool; real work moves back and forth between them.

One recurring point: stationarity (mean, variance and covariances do not depend on time) and weak dependence (distant observations are nearly independent) are what make the law of large numbers and the central limit theorem usable. With a unit root they fail, and ordinary t-tests and regression inference must be redone.

1. Time-Series Regression and Distributed Lags

Intuition. Policies and prices rarely show their full effect at once: a tax change moves fertility slowly, an oil price rise adjusts output month by month. So regressions need lags, and we must separate the effect "in one period", the "cumulative effect" and the "long-run effect of a permanent change".

Static model: y_t=\alpha+x_t'\beta+u_t. "Static" means no explicit lags, not that the variables lack time dependence.

Finite distributed lag (FDL) model:

y_t=\alpha+\sum_{j=0}^{q}\delta_jx_{t-j}+z_t'\lambda+u_t.

Holding other variables' paths fixed:

  • x_t rises by 1 in one period only: the response of y_{t+h} is \delta_h (0\le h\le q), then 0.
  • x_t rises by 1 permanently from t on: the period-h response is \sum_{j=0}^{\min(h,q)}\delta_j, and the long-run effect is \theta=\sum_{j=0}^{q}\delta_j (the long-run multiplier).

The response "in one period" and the cumulative response are different objects.

Standard error of a cumulative effect. Do not add standard errors. With a=(1,\ldots,1)' and \widehat\theta=a'\widehat\delta,

\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat\theta)=a'\widehat V_\delta a,

which includes all covariances. A simpler route is reparametrisation:

y_t=\alpha+\theta x_t+\sum_{j=1}^{q}\delta_j(x_{t-j}-x_t)+z_t'\lambda+u_t,

where the coefficient on x_t is the total effect \theta and the regression reports its standard error directly.

Long-run effect with a lagged dependent variable (supplementary). If

y_t=c+\phi y_{t-1}+\sum_{j=0}^{q}\delta_jx_{t-j}+u_t,\quad|\phi|<1,

comparing the old and new long-run equilibria gives

\frac{\partial\bar y}{\partial\bar x}=\frac{\sum_{j=0}^q\delta_j}{1-\phi}.

The pure-FDL \sum\delta_j cannot be used when y feeds back on itself, and a causal reading of these path effects also requires suitable exogeneity of changes in x.

2. OLS with Time Series: Finite-Sample and Large-Sample Theory

Intuition. In cross sections, random sampling automatically makes regressors independent of the errors. In time series today's error may affect tomorrow's regressor (an inflation shock affects future policy and unemployment). Whether strict exogeneity holds decides how far finite-sample theory goes; when it fails we fall back on large samples and stationarity.

2.1 Finite-sample assumptions TS.1–TS.6

Let y=X\beta+u with X stacking all periods.

Assumption Content Role
TS.1 linear in parameters, correctly specified, fixed coefficients defines the target
TS.2 no perfect collinearity OLS exists uniquely
TS.3 strict exogeneity: E(u_t\mid X)=0 conditional unbiasedness
TS.4 \operatorname{Var}(u_t\mid X)=\sigma^2 usual variance formula
TS.5 \operatorname{Cov}(u_t,u_s\mid X)=0,\ t\ne s usual variance and BLUE
TS.6 errors jointly normal given X exact t/F inference

From \widehat\beta=\beta+(X'X)^{-1}X'u: TS.1–TS.3 give E(\widehat\beta\mid X)=\beta; adding TS.4–TS.5 gives \operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta\mid X)=\sigma^2(X'X)^{-1} with \widehat\sigma^2=\widehat u'\widehat u/(T-k) (k including the intercept). OLS has the smallest variance among linear unbiased estimators (Gauss–Markov); normality is needed only for exact distributions.

2.2 Contemporaneous vs strict exogeneity

  • Contemporaneous exogeneity: E(u_t\mid x_t)=0.
  • Strict exogeneity: the current error is uncorrelated with all past and future regressors, ruling out feedback from today's shock to future regressors.

For y_t=c+\phi y_{t-1}+u_t: even if E(u_t\mid y_{t-1})=0, next period's regressor contains y_t, which contains u_t, so strict exogeneity generally fails — models with lagged dependent variables cannot use the static model's finite-sample unbiasedness.

2.3 Weak stationarity and weak dependence

Covariance stationarity: E(y_t)=\mu, \operatorname{Cov}(y_t,y_{t-k})=\gamma_k, \gamma_0<\infty. It restricts only the first two moments, unlike strict stationarity. Weak dependence: dependence between distant observations is weak enough for LLN/CLT. Stationarity and weak dependence are different requirements.

2.4 Large-sample assumptions and results

Replace the finite-sample conditions with: TS.1′ the process is stationary, weakly dependent and linear in parameters; TS.2′ no perfect collinearity; TS.3′ contemporaneous zero conditional mean; TS.4′, TS.5′ contemporaneous homoskedasticity and suitable absence of serial correlation. Then

\widehat\beta\xrightarrow{p}\beta,\qquad\sqrt T(\widehat\beta-\beta)\Rightarrow N(0,\,Q^{-1}SQ^{-1}),

where Q=E(x_tx_t') and S is the long-run covariance of the score x_tu_t; with homoskedasticity and no autocorrelation it reduces to the usual formula.

Levels of conclusion: finite-sample unbiasedness, consistency, asymptotic normality, validity of usual standard errors and efficiency are different statements. Autocorrelation or heteroskedasticity may break only some; endogeneity breaks consistency itself.

3. Trends, Seasonality and Transformations

Intuition. Two variables that both "grow" (housing investment and house prices, or two unrelated things) look highly correlated because of a common time trend. To ask whether other variables explain fluctuations we must first separate the trend.

Deterministic trends: y_t=a+bt+v_t (linear) or \log y_t=a+bt+v_t (exponential). b is a continuously compounded growth rate; the discrete percentage rate is 100(e^b-1), about 100b for small b.

Detrending and FWL. In the regression of y on x, an intercept and a time trend, the coefficient on x equals the coefficient from regressing the residuals of y on the trend on the residuals of x on the trend. If most of the variation in y is trend, the raw R^2 mostly reflects the trend and says nothing about how well other variables explain fluctuations; when reporting a fit relative to detrended variation, state the denominator.

Seasonality. Monthly data: 11 month dummies plus an intercept (quarterly: 3), avoiding the dummy-variable trap:

y_t=\alpha+x_t'\beta+\sum_{m=2}^{12}\eta_mD_{m,t}+u_t.

This controls deterministic seasonal means, not seasonal dynamics or seasonal unit roots.

Logs, differences and growth rates:

g_t=\Delta\log Y_t\approx\frac{Y_t-Y_{t-1}}{Y_{t-1}}.

For GDP: the level grows visibly; its log is roughly linear in time; the log difference is roughly stationary. The transformations do different jobs:

  • logs compress scale and can ease multiplicative heteroskedasticity, but do not remove a unit root;
  • detrending suits trend stationarity;
  • differencing removes a stochastic trend but may discard long-run relations;
  • choose by combining plots, economics and unit-root tests.

ARIMA. If \Delta^dy_t is ARMA(p,q), then y_t is ARIMA(p,d,q) (used here only as connecting vocabulary; seasonal ARIMA is not developed).

4. AR, MA and ARMA: Dynamic Propagation

Intuition. ARMA writes "how a series depends on its own past" through two simplest mechanisms: AR, where last period's value feeds into this period (memory persists through the state); and MA, where the last few shocks add up directly (memory lasts only finitely many periods).

4.1 White noise and innovations

White noise: zero mean, finite constant variance, uncorrelated across time. Uncorrelated does not mean independent — ARCH errors are uncorrelated in levels but correlated in squares. For forecasting we usually also want E(\varepsilon_t\mid\mathcal I_{t-1})=0.

4.2 AR(1)

y_t=c+\phi y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,\quad|\phi|<1.
\mu=\frac{c}{1-\phi},\quad\gamma_0=\frac{\sigma^2}{1-\phi^2},\quad\gamma_k=\phi^{|k|}\gamma_0,\quad\rho_k=\phi^{|k|}.

Centred, \widetilde y_t=\sum_{j\ge0}\phi^j\varepsilon_{t-j}; the response to one innovation is \partial y_{t+h}/\partial\varepsilon_t=\phi^h. For 0<\phi<1 it decays monotonically, for -1<\phi<0 with alternating signs, for \phi near 1 very slowly, and at \phi=1 we are in unit-root territory (the stationary variance formula no longer applies).

Half-life (0<\phi<1): \log(1/2)/\log\phi, translating "a persistent coefficient" into time. For \phi=0.9 it is about 6.6 periods.

4.3 MA(1): short memory and invertibility

y_t=\mu+\varepsilon_t+\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}.
\operatorname{Var}(y_t)=(1+\theta^2)\sigma^2,\quad\gamma_1=\theta\sigma^2,\quad\gamma_k=0\ (k>1),\quad\rho_1=\frac{\theta}{1+\theta^2}.

A shock has response 1 now, \theta next period and 0 afterwards. Any finite MA is covariance stationary; invertibility is a separate condition: for |\theta|<1, \varepsilon_t=(1+\theta L)^{-1}(y_t-\mu), so past innovations can be recovered from observables, and the MA parameter is pinned down (\theta and 1/\theta give the same ACF).

4.4 General ARMA

\phi(L)y_t=c+\theta(L)\varepsilon_t,\quad\phi(L)=1-\sum_{i=1}^p\phi_iL^i,\quad\theta(L)=1+\sum_{j=1}^q\theta_jL^j.

Causal stationarity requires the roots of the AR polynomial outside the unit circle; invertibility requires the roots of the MA polynomial outside it. Software that reports "inverse roots" requires them inside the unit circle — do not mix the two. Under suitable conditions

y_t-\mu=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\psi_j\varepsilon_{t-j},\quad\psi(L)=\frac{\theta(L)}{\phi(L)},\ \psi_0=1,

and \psi_h describes both propagation of an innovation and multi-step forecast errors. A general ARMA has both ACF and PACF tailing off, so one sample plot rarely identifies the orders uniquely.

5. ACF, PACF and Box–Jenkins Modelling

Intuition. The ACF asks "how correlated are two values k periods apart?"; the PACF asks "how much correlation is left after controlling for all lags in between?". AR memory travels along a chain, so the ACF tails off and the PACF cuts off; MA memory lasts only q periods, so its ACF cuts off.

5.1 Definitions and sample estimates

\rho_k=\frac{\gamma_k}{\gamma_0},\quad\widehat\gamma_k=\frac1T\sum_{t=k+1}^T(y_t-\bar y)(y_{t-k}-\bar y),\quad\widehat\rho_k=\frac{\widehat\gamma_k}{\widehat\gamma_0}.

The PACF \phi_{k,k} is the last coefficient in the regression y_t=c+\phi_{1,k}y_{t-1}+\cdots+\phi_{k,k}y_{t-k}+v_t, estimated separately for each k.

5.2 Theoretical identification patterns

Model Theoretical ACF Theoretical PACF
AR(p) geometric or oscillating tail cuts off after lag p
MA(q) cuts off after lag q tails off
ARMA(p,q) tails off tails off
unit-root candidate sample ACF decays very slowly combine with unit-root tests

"Cutting off" is a population property; a sample plot is never exactly zero beyond some lag. Under white noise a single sample ACF has a rough band of \pm1.96/\sqrt T, which is not a generally valid simultaneous band, and inspecting many lags creates a multiple-comparison problem.

5.3 Information criteria

\mathrm{AIC}=-2\widehat\ell+2k,\qquad\mathrm{BIC}=-2\widehat\ell+k\log T.

For Gaussian ARMA on the same sample, dropping common constants and dividing by T:

\mathrm{AIC}\simeq\log\widehat\sigma^2+\frac{2k}{T},\qquad\mathrm{BIC}\simeq\log\widehat\sigma^2+\frac{k\log T}{T}.

k counts estimated parameters; the convention for the intercept and variance must be consistent across models. Smaller is better; BIC usually favours more parsimonious models than AIC.

5.4 Residual diagnostics and Ljung–Box

Good residuals should look like white noise. Inspect the residual plot, residual ACF/PACF, then squared residuals (is volatility adequately modelled?). Ljung–Box:

Q(m)=T(T+2)\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{\widehat\rho_j^2}{T-j}.

For ARMA residuals it is approximately \chi^2_{m-p-q}. The null is zero autocorrelation at the tested lags; failing to reject does not prove residuals are independent or normal.

5.5 The Box–Jenkins loop

  1. inspect the raw data, frequency, seasonal adjustment, missing values, transformation;
  2. use plots and tests to bring the series to a suitable stationary form;
  3. propose several candidates from ACF/PACF;
  4. estimate; check roots, parameters and residuals;
  5. compare information criteria on the same sample; revise if diagnostics fail;
  6. judge forecasting performance on held-out or rolling forecasts, not only in-sample fit.

6. Residual Autocorrelation: Tests, Modelling and Robust Inference

Intuition. If u_t=\rho u_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t, each observation contributes less "new information" than its T count suggests, and the usual standard errors are wrong. But beware: with a lagged dependent variable, autocorrelation does not just make standard errors inaccurate — it makes OLS inconsistent.

6.1 What autocorrelation breaks

If strict exogeneity still holds, autocorrelation alone does not destroy conditional unbiasedness; under suitable asymptotic conditions and contemporaneous exogeneity consistency can survive. But the usual variance, t/F tests and efficiency claims fail in general.

With a lagged dependent variable: y_{t-1} contains u_{t-1}, and u_t is correlated with u_{t-1}, so y_{t-1} is correlated with u_t — the regressor is endogenous and OLS inconsistent. HAC cannot repair this.

6.2 Tests

  • Residual AR(1) test: regress \widehat u_t=\rho\widehat u_{t-1}+v_t and test \rho=0 (needs strict exogeneity).
  • Durbin–Watson:
    DW=\frac{\sum_{t=2}^T(\widehat u_t-\widehat u_{t-1})^2}{\sum_{t=1}^T\widehat u_t^2}\approx2(1-\widehat\rho).
    Near 2 is compatible with weak first-order autocorrelation, near 0 suggests positive and near 4 negative; the classical test uses bounds d_L,d_U with an inconclusive zone. Not valid with lagged dependent variables.
  • Breusch–Godfrey LM: auxiliary regression of residuals on the original regressors and m lagged residuals,
    \widehat u_t=x_t'a+\sum_{j=1}^m\rho_j\widehat u_{t-j}+v_t,
    test \rho_1=\cdots=\rho_m=0; effective sample size times R^2 is asymptotically \chi^2_m. More suitable than DW for general dynamic regressions.

6.3 Treating it in the model

If y_t=\beta_0+\beta_1x_t+u_t and u_t=\rho u_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t, then

y_t=\beta_0(1-\rho)+\rho y_{t-1}+\beta_1x_t-\rho\beta_1x_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,

where the last coefficient is nonlinearly constrained by the others; feasible GLS, nonlinear least squares or ML can be used. Also check for omitted dynamics, trends, seasonality or structural change — do not add lags or differences without principle just to make a test insignificant.

6.4 HAC / Newey–West

HAC gives a covariance estimate for OLS that is robust to heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation; it does not change the point estimate. With g_t=x_tu_t:

Q=E(x_tx_t'),\quad S=\sum_{j=-\infty}^{\infty}E(g_tg_{t-j}'),\quad\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\beta)\approx\frac1TQ^{-1}SQ^{-1}.

Newey–West estimates S with truncated, weighted sample autocovariances:

\widehat S=\widehat\Gamma_0+\sum_{j=1}^{b}w_j(\widehat\Gamma_j+\widehat\Gamma_j'),\quad w_j=1-\frac{j}{b+1}\ \text{(Bartlett)}.

b is a bandwidth, not the model's AR order. Three cases differ:

Case What to do
correct, exogenous target; errors merely dependent HAC improves inference
omission makes regressors correlated with errors fix the model, use IV; HAC does not cure bias
goal is forecasting the whole conditional distribution model mean and variance directly

The direction of standard-error bias depends on the joint dependence of regressors and errors; it is not "always understated".

7. Heteroskedasticity, ARCH and GARCH

Intuition. The level of asset returns is nearly unpredictable, but their volatility is predictable: large moves tend to follow large moves (volatility clustering). ARCH/GARCH write the conditional variance as a function of past shocks.

7.1 Conditional and unconditional variance

h_t=\operatorname{Var}(u_t\mid\mathcal I_{t-1}).

h_t can vary with past information while the unconditional variance \operatorname{Var}(u_t) stays constant — clustering and covariance stationarity can coexist. A different case is a fixed variance break across regimes or crises, which is not stationary GARCH dynamics. Heteroskedasticity also does not imply E(u_t\mid x_t)\ne0.

7.2 ARCH and GARCH

u_t=\sqrt{h_t}\,z_t,\quad E(z_t\mid\mathcal I_{t-1})=0,\ E(z_t^2\mid\mathcal I_{t-1})=1.

ARCH(q): h_t=\omega+\sum_{i=1}^q\alpha_iu_{t-i}^2, \omega>0,\alpha_i\ge0. For ARCH(1) with \alpha_1<1 the unconditional variance is E(u_t^2)=\omega/(1-\alpha_1) (not the conditional variance in each period). ARCH makes u_t uncorrelated while u_t^2 is autocorrelated.

GARCH(1,1):

h_t=\omega+\alpha u_{t-1}^2+\beta h_{t-1},
\omega>0,\ \alpha,\beta\ge0,\ \alpha+\beta<1,\qquad E(u_t^2)=\frac{\omega}{1-\alpha-\beta}.

\alpha is the reaction to new shocks, \beta the carry-over of past variance, and \alpha+\beta near 1 means highly persistent volatility. (Second-order stationarity, strict stationarity and existence of higher moments are different conditions.)

7.3 Tests and diagnostics

ARCH-LM: auxiliary regression \widehat u_t^2=a_0+\sum_{j=1}^qa_j\widehat u_{t-j}^2+v_t, test all a_j=0, T_{eff}R^2\overset a\sim\chi_q^2. Specify the mean model first. After estimation inspect standardised residuals \widehat z_t=\widehat u_t/\sqrt{\widehat h_t}: their ACF checks leftover mean dynamics, the ACF of their squares leftover volatility dynamics.

7.4 Case: NYSE daily returns

1988-01-01 to 2001-12-21, about 3461 observations (a historical case).

Model Result AIC / BIC
ARCH(5) five lags of squared shocks significant, but standardised squared residuals still have long-lag correlation -6.8215 / -6.8090
GARCH(1,1) \widehat\omega=1.06\times10^{-6}, \widehat\alpha=0.0674, \widehat\beta=0.9197 -6.8680 / -6.8609

\widehat\alpha+\widehat\beta=0.987: very persistent. GARCH(1,1) is preferred not because the mean regression has a high R^2 but because the conditional variance and diagnostics fit better: the classic "mean hard to predict, volatility easy to predict".

7.5 Forecasting variance

In GARCH(1,1), after seeing u_t: h_{t+1|t}=\omega+\alpha u_t^2+\beta h_t, and further out

h_{t+k|t}=\bar h+(\alpha+\beta)^{k-1}(h_{t+1|t}-\bar h),\quad\bar h=\frac{\omega}{1-\alpha-\beta}.

The conditional mean of returns may hardly move, but risk forecasts jump after a large recent shock and then decay; in the NYSE example \alpha+\beta is so high that the decay is very slow.

8. Unit Roots, Stochastic Trends and DF/ADF Tests

Intuition. After a shock some series return to their trend line (trend stationary); others carry the shock permanently into the future (random walk). The two look alike in plots but differ completely statistically: the first can be detrended, the second must be differenced, and the ordinary t-test is useless for the second.

8.1 Trend stationary vs difference stationary

Process Example How to make stationary Long-run effect of one innovation
trend stationary y_t=a+bt+v_t, v_t stationary detrend deviations from trend die out
random walk y_t=y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t first difference innovation enters the level permanently
random walk with drift y_t=d+y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t difference; mean d same

A random walk with fixed initial value: y_t=y_0+\sum_{j=1}^t\varepsilon_j, E(y_t)=y_0, \operatorname{Var}(y_t)=t\sigma^2. A constant mean can still be non-stationary because the variance grows. The IRF to an innovation is 1 at every h. Its correlation \operatorname{Corr}(y_t,y_{t-k})=\sqrt{(t-k)/t} depends on t and tends to 1 for large t, so the stationary ACF definition does not apply.

8.2 Why the usual t-test fails

After estimating y_t=\phi y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t we cannot test \phi=1 with standard critical values: under the unit-root null the estimator and the t-statistic have non-standard limiting distributions, which change with the intercept and trend. Fitting a random walk with a deterministic trend and treating the residuals as an ordinary cycle is also dangerous — low-frequency stochastic drift gets mistaken for a linear trend.

8.3 The Dickey–Fuller test

Write the AR(1) as

\Delta y_t=d_t'\eta+\gamma y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,\quad\gamma=\phi-1,

and test H_0:\gamma=0 against the left-tailed alternative (stationary or trend stationary). Approximate asymptotic critical values:

Deterministic terms in the test regression 5% 1%
none -1.94 -2.57
intercept -2.86 -3.43
intercept + linear trend -3.41 -3.96

A more negative statistic supports rejecting the unit root. Do not switch deterministic terms arbitrarily to get the conclusion you want.

8.4 ADF: more general dynamics

\Delta y_t=d_t'\eta+\gamma y_{t-1}+\sum_{j=1}^{k}\lambda_j\Delta y_{t-j}+\varepsilon_t.

Lagged differences make the regression errors approximately serially uncorrelated. For AR(2): y_t=\phi_1y_{t-1}+\phi_2y_{t-2}+\varepsilon_t=(\phi_1+\phi_2)y_{t-1}-\phi_2\Delta y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t, so a unit root means \phi_1+\phi_2=1. Too few lags: correlated residuals and size distortion; too many: lost power. One can start from a large maximum lag and prune from the top (monthly data are often started at 12 — a teaching choice only).

Reading the table: with an intercept, \widehat\gamma=-0.08 and standard error 0.03 give \tau_{ADF}\approx-2.67>-2.86, so the unit root is not rejected; using the normal left-tail value -1.645 would wrongly reject.

Failing to reject a unit root is not proof of one: highly persistent stationary processes, short samples and structural breaks make the two hard to tell apart. Report together: levels or logs, deterministic terms, lag order, effective sample, statistic, critical value and residual diagnostics.

8.5 Case: US inflation persistence

1960–2010, 204 quarters of seasonally adjusted CPI inflation (a historical case). ACF significant for the first 7 lags; PACF points to about 3 main lags. The ADF statistic with an intercept and 2 lags is -3.078 (rejects), with 4 lags -2.76 (does not); later modelling assumes a highly persistent I(0) for later modelling, rather than claiming stationarity has been decisively proven. Candidates AR(3), AR(4), ARMA(3,1), AR(6) and a sparse AR(6) (lags 1, 2, 3, 6 only; coefficients about 0.270,0.216,0.242,0.125): AR(3) still has residual correlation; the sparse model is slightly preferred by AIC and AR(3) by BIC, and both show high persistence.

9. Forecasting, Forecast Errors and Model Comparison

Intuition. A forecast is not just a number: it must say how uncertain it is and prove itself out of sample. How fast the conditional mean reverts and how fast uncertainty accumulates both come from the model's dynamics.

9.1 Optimal forecasts

Under squared-error loss \widehat y_{T+h|T}=E(y_{T+h}\mid\mathcal I_T) with error e_{T+h|T}=y_{T+h}-\widehat y_{T+h|T}. If only linear forecasts are allowed, use the linear projection; for non-Gaussian data they may differ.

9.2 Forecasts and error variances from the MA representation

If y_t-\mu=\sum_{j\ge0}\psi_j\varepsilon_{t-j}, with known parameters and recoverable innovations,

\widehat y_{T+h|T}=\mu+\sum_{j=h}^{\infty}\psi_j\varepsilon_{T+h-j},\qquad\sigma_h^2=\sigma^2\sum_{j=0}^{h-1}\psi_j^2.
  • MA(1): \widehat y_{T+1|T}=\mu+\theta\varepsilon_T, and \mu for h\ge2; error variance \sigma^2 (h=1), (1+\theta^2)\sigma^2 (h\ge2). A general MA(q) reverts to the mean for h>q with error variance equal to the unconditional variance.
  • AR(1): \widehat y_{T+h|T}=\mu+\phi^h(y_T-\mu), \sigma_h^2=\sigma^2\frac{1-\phi^{2h}}{1-\phi^2}.
  • Random walk: forecast stays at the current level, error variance h\sigma^2.

An AR(p) can be forecast recursively, replacing unknown future lags by their forecasts.

Worked example. AR(1) with \mu=10,\phi=0.8,\sigma=2,y_T=15: \widehat y_{T+1|T}=14, \widehat y_{T+2|T}=13.2; error variances 4 and 4(1+0.64)=6.56; the two-step 95% interval is 13.2\pm1.96\sqrt{6.56}=[8.18,18.22]; as h\to\infty the variance tends to 4/(1-0.64)=11.11. MA(1) with \mu=10,\theta=0.5,\sigma=2,\varepsilon_T=4: forecast 12 for one step and 10 afterwards, error variances 4 and 5.

9.3 Intervals and accuracy

With normal innovations, a correct model and ignoring parameter uncertainty, the pointwise interval is \widehat y_{T+h|T}\pm1.96\,\sigma_h. It is a pointwise approximation, not a 95% simultaneous band for the whole future path. Accuracy:

\mathrm{RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Ne_i^2};

it is more informative to fix the horizon and average over many forecast origins.

Diebold–Mariano: loss differential d_i=e_{1,i}^2-e_{2,i}^2, \bar d=\frac1N\sum d_i, and the full statistic

DM=\frac{\bar d}{\sqrt{\widehat S_d/N}},

where \widehat S_d is a long-run variance estimate of the loss differential (multi-step errors overlap, so correlation must be accounted for); the mean \bar d alone is not a complete test.

9.4 Rolling evaluation and back-transformation

Evaluate by time-splitting: move the forecast origin forward, using only data before each origin; an expanding window keeps all past data, a rolling window keeps a fixed length of recent data, and which is better depends on parameter stability. All models must use the same origins, horizons and target variable, and standardisation, trend estimation and order selection must use training data only.

If the model forecasts g_t=\Delta\log Y_t, then \widehat{\log Y}_{T+h|T}=\log Y_T+\sum_{j=1}^h\widehat g_{T+j|T}, and the variance of the cumulated error includes covariances between period errors. If the log level is conditionally N(m_h,v_h), the conditional mean of the level is \exp(m_h+v_h/2) and its median \exp(m_h); in general E(e^X)\ne e^{E(X)}.

9.5 Case: Canadian employment index

Quarterly, seasonally adjusted, 1962Q1–1993Q4, 128 observations, first-order sample autocorrelation about 0.949.

Model Key diagnostics AIC / BIC
MA(4) DW about 1.247; residuals still cyclical with AR structure AIC about 2.203
AR(2) coefficients about 1.4388,-0.4765; inverse roots about 0.92, 0.52; Q test does not reject 0.7617 / 0.8285
ARMA(3,1) diagnostics also fine; MA coefficient about 0.971 0.7607 / 0.8721

AIC slightly prefers ARMA(3,1), BIC prefers AR(2), and the simpler AR(2) is favoured. A single AR(2) coefficient above 1 does not mean instability — check the roots. After 4 periods the MA(4) forecast returns to the mean immediately, which looks too quick after a recession; the AR(2) recovers more slowly and fits the realised path better — but this is one sample, not a proof that "AR always beats MA".

10. Spurious Regression, Cointegration and Error Correction

Intuition. Two unrelated, drifting random walks often produce a "highly significant" levels regression (spurious regression). Yet some variables (consumption and income, long and short rates, exchange rates and relative prices) drift individually but are tied together by a long-run relation: a combination of them is stationary. That is cointegration; it brings "long-run equilibrium" into dynamic models.

10.1 Three misleading regressions

  1. two independent I(1) series in levels: apparently significant t and high R^2 but invalid inference;
  2. two deterministically trending variables with the trend omitted: spurious correlation;
  3. even stationary data, with omitted dynamics and strongly correlated errors under wrong standard errors, can mislead.

A low DW suggests strongly correlated residuals but is not a sufficient criterion for cointegration.

10.2 Definition

If y_t,x_t are both I(1) and there are coefficients such that

z_t=y_t-a-\beta x_t\sim I(0),

the two are cointegrated; z_t is the deviation from the long-run relation. Multivariate form: Y_t\sim I(1) and a non-zero vector b with b'Y_t\sim I(0). Cointegration is a restriction on common stochastic trends; it does not give coefficients a causal meaning. Common-trend example: y_{1t}=\beta\tau_t+u_{1t}, y_{2t}=\tau_t+u_{2t}, \tau_t=\tau_{t-1}+v_t; then y_{1t}-\beta y_{2t} is stationary.

10.3 Known and unknown cointegrating vectors

  • Vector given by theory: construct the combination and test it for a unit root. Example: the 6-month minus 3-month Treasury spread r_{6,t}-r_{3,t}, with a test statistic of about -7.78 rejecting a unit root in the spread; the real exchange rate s_t-p_t+p_t^* is another.
  • Engle–Granger two-step: (1) levels regression y_{1t}=a+b_2y_{2t}+\cdots+z_t; (2) unit-root test on the estimated residuals \widehat z_t; (3) use the special critical values for cointegration residuals, not the ordinary ADF table (OLS has already made the residuals as small as possible, shifting the distribution).

Asymptotic critical values, for example: with intercept and two variables 1%/5%/10% are -3.90/-3.34/-3.04; with a linear trend -4.32/-3.78/-3.50; for 3, 4, 5 variables the 5% values are about -3.74/-4.10/-4.42. Match the number of variables, deterministic terms and sample when using them.

10.4 Super-consistency is not a licence

The long-run slope of a cointegrating regression converges at rate T (not \sqrt T) — "super-consistency" — but the limiting distribution depends on the correlation between residuals and regressors, serial dependence and deterministic terms, so ordinary t values cannot be read as standard normal. Order of checks: integration orders and cointegration first, then whether the regressor in question is I(0) or I(1), then exogeneity and distributional conditions; reparametrising into stationary combinations can make some coefficients amenable to standard asymptotics.

10.5 Case: Stock–Watson's "two econometricians"

Simulate the true mechanism: Y_t=Y_t^P+Y_t^T, Y_t^P=Y_{t-1}^P+u_t, Y_t^T\sim iid\,N(0,1); C_t=Y_t^P; P_t=P_{t-1}+v_t, innovations independent. Consumption and income share the permanent component, and consumption does not depend on the price level.

  • The first researcher finds a significant price effect, a significant deterministic trend in consumption, a coefficient of about 0.28 of differenced consumption on differenced income, and apparent predictive power of lagged consumption. The problems: a non-cointegrated levels spurious regression; a stochastic trend mistaken for a deterministic one; differenced income contains transitory income and so suffers measurement-error-like attenuation; and the unit-root test uses the ordinary t distribution.
  • The second researcher models the long-run relation in levels with lagged dynamics, gets a long-run coefficient of consumption on income of about 0.94, and finds prices do not predict consumption — closer to the true mechanism. Even a long-run slope close to 1 does not license an unconditional ordinary t-test that it is below 1.

10.6 Error-correction models (ECM/VECM)

\Delta y_t=\lambda(y_{t-1}-a-\beta x_{t-1})+\sum_i\phi_i\Delta y_{t-i}+\sum_j\psi_j\Delta x_{t-j}+u_t.

The bracket is last period's deviation from the long-run relation; if the adjustment of y corrects deviations stably, typically \lambda<0. Derivation from an ARDL(1,1): subtract y_{t-1} from y_t=c+\phi y_{t-1}+\delta_0x_t+\delta_1x_{t-1}+u_t and use x_t=\Delta x_t+x_{t-1}:

\Delta y_t=c+(\phi-1)y_{t-1}+(\delta_0+\delta_1)x_{t-1}+\delta_0\Delta x_t+u_t.

With \lambda=\phi-1, a=c/(1-\phi), \beta=(\delta_0+\delta_1)/(1-\phi) this is \Delta y_t=\lambda(y_{t-1}-a-\beta x_{t-1})+\delta_0\Delta x_t+u_t. The long-run slope \beta is not the contemporaneous coefficient \delta_0, and modelling only differences discards "how far off the long-run relation we are". Example: if last period y was 10 units above the long-run relation and \lambda=-0.2, the correction term contributes -2 this period.

VECM: rewriting a VAR(p),

\Delta Y_t=c+\Pi Y_{t-1}+\sum_{i=1}^{p-1}\Gamma_i\Delta Y_{t-i}+u_t,\quad\Pi=\sum_{i=1}^pA_i-I,\ \Gamma_i=-\sum_{j=i+1}^pA_j.

If 0<\operatorname{rank}\Pi=r<n then \Pi=\alpha\beta', with \beta the cointegrating vectors and \alpha the adjustment speeds. An n-dimensional I(1) system with r cointegrating relations has n-r common stochastic trends; the scale of a cointegrating vector is not unique, so normalise before comparing coefficients. r=0: model differences; 0<r<n: VECM; r=n: the levels system is itself stationary. With several relations one EG residual regression cannot reveal the whole cointegration space (Johansen rank tests are not developed here).

11. VARs: Systems, Estimation and Stability

Intuition. When variables feed back on each other (money and income, inflation and rates), a contemporaneous endogenous variable in a single equation is correlated with the error. A VAR regresses each variable on the past of all variables, letting the data describe "who moves first and who follows"; it is the workhorse of multivariate forecasting, but it does not tell you the economic meaning of each residual.

11.1 Reduced-form VAR

Y_t=c+A_1Y_{t-1}+\cdots+A_pY_{t-p}+u_t,\quad E(u_t\mid\mathcal I_{t-1})=0,\ E(u_tu_t')=\Sigma_u.

Every equation has the same lags, so equation-by-equation OLS is consistent. With x_t=(1,Y_{t-1}',\ldots,Y_{t-p}')', \widehat{\mathsf B}=(\mathsf X'\mathsf X)^{-1}\mathsf X'\mathsf Y. Innovations may be correlated across equations within a period. With an intercept each equation has 1+np coefficients, the system n(1+np) mean parameters plus n(n+1)/2 covariance elements — more variables and lags quickly use up the sample. OLS with lagged dependent variables is not guaranteed unbiased in finite samples.

11.2 Companion form

With Z_t=(Y_t',Y_{t-1}',\ldots,Y_{t-p+1}')', Z_t=d+\mathcal AZ_{t-1}+v_t,

\mathcal A=\begin{pmatrix}A_1&A_2&\cdots&A_p\\I&0&\cdots&0\\0&I&\cdots&0\\\vdots&&\ddots&\vdots\end{pmatrix},\quad v_t=(u_t',0',\ldots,0')'.

For a two-variable VAR(2) stacked as (y_{1t},y_{2t},y_{1,t-1},y_{2,t-1})' the companion matrix is \begin{pmatrix}a_{11}&a_{12}&b_{11}&b_{12}\\a_{21}&a_{22}&b_{21}&b_{22}\\1&0&0&0\\0&1&0&0\end{pmatrix}; the lower rows just move current variables into next period's lag positions. The companion matrix is np\times np.

11.3 Stability and the MA form

If all eigenvalues of the companion matrix lie inside the unit circle the system has a causal stationary representation. For a VAR(p) the mean is \mu=(I-\sum A_i)^{-1}c and

Y_t=\mu+\sum_{h=0}^{\infty}\Psi_hu_{t-h},\quad\Psi_0=I,\ \Psi_h=\sum_{i=1}^{\min(p,h)}A_i\Psi_{h-i}.

For VAR(1) \Psi_h=A_1^h. The VAR(1) forecast is \widehat Y_{T+h|T}=\mu+A_1^h(Y_T-\mu) and the H-step forecast-error covariance V_H=\sum_{j=0}^{H-1}\Psi_j\Sigma_u\Psi_j'. Note that \Sigma_u need not be diagonal: the data tell us the total forecast-error variance but not how much each economic shock contributes.

11.4 The line between forecasting and structural analysis

A reduced-form VAR can forecast multivariately without giving each residual an economic name. To answer "how much does output fall after an exogenous rate rise" we must determine which part of the innovations is the policy shock (Chapter 12). Granger predictability tests whether all lags of a variable are jointly zero in another equation — whether it adds forecasting information — which is not structural causality.

11.5 Diagnostic order

First fix the economic definition of the variables, levels/differences and frequency, then judge unit roots and cointegration; choose lags by information criteria, sample size, institutional background and residual correlation; check companion roots, cross-equation innovation covariances, outliers and parameter stability. With unit roots in a levels VAR the coefficients can still be estimated and used for some forecasts, but the finite long-run multipliers and all usual inference of a stable VAR do not carry over; to study common stochastic trends use a specification compatible with cointegration and deterministic terms.

12. SVARs: Identification and Impulse Responses

Intuition. A reduced-form innovation u_t mixes several structural shocks: in the month oil prices rise we cannot tell whether it is a supply disruption, global demand or precautionary demand. Separating them needs more than data — extra economic assumptions (identification).

12.1 Structural and reduced forms

BY_t=a+\sum_{i=1}^p\Gamma_iY_{t-i}+\varepsilon_t,\quad E(\varepsilon_t\varepsilon_t')=D\text{ (diagonal)}.

Premultiplying by B^{-1}: A_i=B^{-1}\Gamma_i, u_t=B^{-1}\varepsilon_t, \Sigma_u=B^{-1}D(B^{-1})'. Normalising the structural shocks to unit variance: u_t=C\epsilon_t, E(\epsilon_t\epsilon_t')=I, \Sigma_u=CC'. Two-dimensional example: B=\begin{pmatrix}1&-b_{12}\\-b_{21}&1\end{pmatrix}, B^{-1}=\frac1{1-b_{12}b_{21}}\begin{pmatrix}1&b_{12}\\b_{21}&1\end{pmatrix}, invertible iff 1-b_{12}b_{21}\ne0; each reduced-form innovation mixes both structural shocks with feedback factor 1/(1-b_{12}b_{21}).

12.2 Why identification is not automatic

\Sigma_u has only n(n+1)/2 distinct elements while C has n^2 unknowns, so after normalisation one generally needs n(n-1)/2 suitable independent restrictions (only a necessary counting condition; a rank condition must also hold). For any orthogonal matrix Q, (CQ)(CQ)'=CC': the same innovation covariance is compatible with different structural shocks.

12.3 Cholesky (short-run, recursive) identification

Assume the impact matrix C is lower triangular and take the Cholesky factor of \Sigma_u=CC' (normally with a positive diagonal to fix signs). With ordering (\Delta y_t,\pi_t,i_t): output growth does not respond within the period to inflation or policy shocks; inflation responds to output shocks but not policy shocks within the period; the interest rate responds to output and inflation within the period. This is the timing assumption "real activity and prices are slow, policy is fast"; putting the policy variable first instead means the policy does not react to others within the period. The Cholesky factor is unique given the ordering, which is not the same as economic causality being unique; changing the order changes the structural shocks while the reduced-form fit and forecasts remain the same.

Worked example. \Sigma_u=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&5\end{pmatrix} gives C=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\1&2\end{pmatrix}. \epsilon_{1t}=u_{1t}/2, \epsilon_{2t}=(u_{2t}-u_{1t}/2)/2: a one-s.d. first shock moves y_1 by 2 and y_2 by 1 on impact; the second leaves y_1 unchanged and moves y_2 by 2. With A_1=\begin{pmatrix}0.5&0.2\\0&0.4\end{pmatrix}: \Theta_1=A_1C=\begin{pmatrix}1.2&0.4\\0.4&0.8\end{pmatrix} — the second shock has zero impact on y_1 but 0.4 next period: a contemporaneous zero restriction does not make later responses zero.

12.4 Structural IRF, cumulative responses and FEVD

Y_t=\mu+\sum_{h=0}^{\infty}\Theta_h\epsilon_{t-h},\quad\Theta_h=\Psi_hC,\quad\Theta_{ij,h}=\frac{\partial Y_{i,t+h}}{\partial\epsilon_{j,t}}.

Impact response \Theta_0=C; in VAR(1) \Theta_h=A_1^hC. Cumulative response \Theta^{cum}_{ij}(H)=\sum_{h=0}^H\Theta_{ij,h}: if the variable is a log growth rate this is the change in the log level. FEVD: for unit-variance uncorrelated structural shocks the share of variable i's H-step forecast-error variance due to shock j is

\frac{\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\Theta_{ij,h}^2}{\sum_{k=1}^n\sum_{h=0}^{H-1}\Theta_{ik,h}^2}.

It depends on identification just as IRFs do. IRF confidence bands must reflect the estimation uncertainty of the VAR parameters, the innovation covariance and the identification parameters (delta method or bootstrap); pointwise bands are not simultaneous bands for the whole response curve.

Units of a shock: a one-unit shock, a one-s.d. shock and a shock that raises the rate by 25 basis points cannot be compared across charts without a common scale and sign. To normalise the policy variable's impact to 25 bp, rescale the whole response in proportion to that variable's impact response (provided it is not zero).

12.5 Case: Kilian's oil-price shocks

A three-variable monthly VAR: Z_t=(\Delta prod_t,rea_t,rpo_t)' (oil production growth, global real activity, real oil price) with 24 lags. Identification: oil production does not respond within the month to demand or price shocks; global activity responds within the month to supply but not to oil-specific demand shocks; the oil price responds to all shocks within the month; the remaining third shock is interpreted as oil-specific demand (e.g. precautionary demand). Typical results: supply disruptions cause small, temporary price changes; global commodity demand growth causes delayed but more persistent increases; oil-specific demand causes immediate, large and persistent increases; the post-2000 rise is attributed mostly to global demand. The lesson: the same oil-price rise can come from different shocks with different effects on other macro variables.

13. Long-Run Restrictions and Blanchard–Quah Identification

Intuition. Short-run identification puts zero restrictions on the "current period", which requires confidence about instantaneous reactions; long-run identification uses macro-theory neutrality propositions — e.g. "demand shocks do not permanently change output" — to restrict cumulative effects.

13.1 Long-run responses

In a stable VAR \Psi_h\to0 but

\Psi(1)=\sum_{h=0}^\infty\Psi_h=\Big(I-\sum_{i=1}^pA_i\Big)^{-1}

is not zero. The structural cumulative long-run impact is \Theta(1)=\Psi(1)C. Short-run identification restricts C=\Theta_0; long-run identification restricts \Theta(1). Long-run neutrality is normally a statement about particular shocks and particular variable levels, not "all demand shocks are irrelevant for all variables in the long run".

13.2 Blanchard–Quah

X_t=(\Delta\log GDP_t,U_t)' (U_t the unemployment rate), with structural shocks to aggregate supply and aggregate demand, uncorrelated. Assume demand shocks have no long-run effect on the output level:

\sum_{h=0}^{\infty}\Theta_{\Delta y,AD,h}=0.

Responses of output growth and unemployment may vanish period by period, while supply shocks can leave a permanent mark on the output level. What is restricted is the cumulative sum of growth-rate responses, not that demand shocks have zero impact on output growth in the current period.

13.3 The computation chain

Long-run covariance \Lambda=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}\operatorname{Cov}(X_t,X_{t-k})=\Psi(1)\Sigma_u\Psi(1)' (not the ordinary \operatorname{Var}(X_t)); for unit-variance structural shocks \Lambda=\Theta(1)\Theta(1)'.

  1. estimate A_i,\Sigma_u and verify stability;
  2. M=I-\sum A_i, \Psi(1)=M^{-1};
  3. \Lambda=\Psi(1)\Sigma_u\Psi(1)';
  4. impose a lower-triangular long-run response matrix from economics and take the Cholesky factor \Lambda=LL';
  5. \Theta(1)=L and recover C=ML (=\Psi(1)^{-1}\Theta(1));
  6. \Theta_h=\Psi_hC and check \Sigma_u=CC'.

Note that L is the long-run impact matrix and cannot be used directly as the impact matrix C.

Why the long-run covariance differs from the ordinary variance. For a scalar AR(1) x_t=\phi x_{t-1}+u_t: \operatorname{Var}(x_t)=\sigma^2/(1-\phi^2) while \Lambda=\sum_k\gamma_k=\sigma^2/(1-\phi)^2. With \phi=0.5,\sigma^2=1 they are 4/3 and 4: the latter includes cross-period autocovariances, relevant to the uncertainty of sample means and low-frequency accumulated changes.

Example: growth responses vanish but the level response is permanent. If a shock's responses of log output growth are 0.5,0.25,0.125,\ldots, each tends to zero but the long-run level change is the geometric sum 1; another shock with responses 0.5,-0.5,0,\ldots sums to zero, so its long-run level effect is zero. BQ's restriction corresponds to the latter cumulative property.

13.4 Limitations

Long-run restrictions rest on low-frequency features and are sensitive to lag order, sample period, near-unit roots and structural change; restrictions supplied by theory need not hold in every historical regime; short- and long-run identification can give different answers. Long-run restrictions are not "more causal" than short-run ones — the identifying assumption just sits in a different place. Cointegration concerns stationary long-run combinations of variables, whereas long-run SVAR restrictions concern the cumulative effects of a structural shock; they are different.

14. Macro Shocks: Narrative, High-Frequency and External Instruments

Intuition. Most policy-variable movements are reactions to economic conditions (the central bank hikes because it sees overheating), so "hikes and output rise together" does not show that tightening is expansionary. We want variation "outside the rule". Chapters 12–13 put identification inside the system; this chapter finds information outside: historical records, financial-market reactions to announcements and external instruments.

14.1 Four identification strategies

Method Source of information Main condition Main risk
short-run zeros contemporaneous covariances and timing inside the system some variables do not respond within the period ordering, frequency, assumptions on instantaneous reactions
long-run zeros long-run economic theory some cumulative effects are zero low-frequency estimation, validity of theory
narrative / high-frequency series historical records, announcement windows, financial prices constructed series suitably independent of other shocks expectations, information effects, simultaneous events
external instruments proxies for the shock outside the system relevance and exclusion weak instruments, measurement contamination, coverage

A structural shock is an original, economically meaningful, exogenous force uncorrelated with other structural shocks; reduced-form innovations, structural shocks, measured proxies for shocks and instruments are different objects.

14.2 The narrative approach

Use policy records to identify the reasons and dates of changes (the early Romer–Romer work on disinflationary tightenings). The problem: the tightening may be precisely a systematic reaction to expected inflation, so a narrative does not guarantee exogeneity; one must say which information was removed, why policy changed, and whether it directly affects the outcome.

14.3 High-frequency surprises

\Delta r_t=\Delta r_t^{expected}+\Delta r_t^{surprise}.

The expected part is already in prices, so comparing total announcement-day changes with asset returns can wrongly suggest policy has no effect. Kuttner measures the surprise with current-month fed funds futures:

\Delta r_t^{surprise}\approx\frac{m}{m-d}(f_d^0-f_{d-1}^0),

with m the days in the month and d the announcement day; the contract settles on the monthly average effective rate, hence the remaining-days adjustment (month-ends, other contract definitions or windows need separate treatment — do not copy mechanically). After the split the unexpected part still has a clear effect on bond yields.

Event study: R_t=\beta_0+\beta_1\Delta r_t^{surprise}+e_t. In Jansen–Zervou the full-sample \widehat\beta_1\approx-3.869 (t=-2.485, 149 observations): a 1 percentage point (100 bp) surprise rise lowers same-day stock returns by about 3.869 percentage points (interpretation depends on the return units). Subsample coefficients vary widely:
