14.4 External instruments and Proxy SVAR

With u_t=C\epsilon_t, an external series z_t identifies the first shock if

E(z_t\epsilon_{1t})\ne0,\qquad E(z_t\epsilon_{jt})=0\ (j\ne1).

Then E(u_tz_t)=C_{\cdot1}E(\epsilon_{1t}z_t): the covariance vector with z_t identifies the direction of the first column of C, and a scale must still be set (e.g. "policy rate rises by 100 bp on impact"). With q=E(u_tz_t) and q_1\ne0,

b=\frac{q}{q_1}=\frac{c_1}{c_{11}},\quad b_1=1,

and \Psi_hb gives the dynamic response normalised to "the policy variable rises by one data unit on impact", with no need to call the shock a one-s.d. shock. To recover the unit-variance column (assuming \Sigma_u positive definite and C invertible), c_1=b/\sqrt{b'\Sigma_u^{-1}b}. A single proxy typically identifies only the target column, not the meaning of the other shocks.

Example: the policy variable is in percentage points, \operatorname{Cov}(u_x,z)=0.02, \operatorname{Cov}(u_y,z)=-0.06; the relative response of y to the policy variable is -3. Normalising to a 25 bp (0.25 pp) rate rise gives an impact response of -0.75 data units for y (if y=100\log Y, about a 0.75% fall in the level).

Why regressing directly on a noisy proxy attenuates. If y_t=\theta\epsilon_t+v_t but we observe only z_t=\epsilon_t+\nu_t, the population OLS coefficient of y_t on z_t is

\beta_{OLS}=\theta\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_t)}{\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_t)+\operatorname{Var}(\nu_t)}<\theta.

"Exogenous but noisy" does not automatically make the direct regression give the true unit-shock effect; used as an instrument, the noise mostly affects relevance and precision and, under suitable orthogonality, causes no such attenuation. Using a narrative series directly and using it as an IV are two practices that each need their own argument.

14.5 Instrument validity and practical checks

Relevance and exclusion are both needed: a strong first stage does not prove the instrument is uncontaminated by other shocks, and a plausible economic story does not guarantee a strong first stage in the sample (the noisier, the weaker). The first-stage F should be high, but no single threshold is universal; with serial correlation or heteroskedasticity use compatible robust diagnostics. Also check: whether the window contains only one kind of news (target-rate surprise, path surprise, information effects mixed?); the rule for aggregating intraday/daily data to monthly or quarterly, and whether event-free months are zero or missing; and the difference between contemporaneous and cross-period orthogonality — a Proxy VAR's moment condition identifies the impact column, and if the instrument also predicts policy changes in advance, using it in a long-horizon LP-IV may violate the horizon-specific exclusion condition.

15. Local Projections and LP-IV

Intuition. A VAR first estimates a dynamic system and then iterates to get all horizons — one misspecification propagates through the iteration. A local projection (Jordà) is more direct: for each h, regress future y_{t+h} on today's shock. It relies less on the dynamic specification but uses up sample information at every horizon.

15.1 Definition

For an identified shock s_t, estimate separately for each h=0,1,\ldots,H

y_{i,t+h}=a_h+\theta_{i,h}s_t+\Gamma_h'W_t+\xi_{i,t+h}.

\theta_{i,h} is the IRF at that horizon; W_t contains a constant, trends, lags of the outcome and other variables, lags of the shock, etc. A causal reading depends on the shock's exogeneity and the control set — it does not become valid merely because LP is used.

Comparison VAR IRF LP IRF
parameters the same system dynamics jointly restrict all horizons each horizon estimated separately
if correctly specified uses system restrictions, more efficient typically uses more sample information
misspecification dynamic misspecification propagates through iteration fewer cross-horizon restrictions, but can still be misspecified
curve usually smooth usually jagged, wider bands
extensions large systems complicated easy to add IV, nonlinearity, state dependence

These are common features, not an ordering guaranteed in every sample; with compatible population dynamics and the same identification both target the same IRF, and in finite samples they differ through specification and estimation error.

15.2 HAC and overlapping errors

For h>0 future errors of adjacent origins overlap, so LP residuals typically have MA-type correlation. Example: for stable y_t=ay_{t-1}+\epsilon_t the two-step errors e_{t+2|t}=a\epsilon_{t+1}+\epsilon_{t+2} and e_{t+3|t+1}=a\epsilon_{t+2}+\epsilon_{t+3} share \epsilon_{t+2}. Hence Newey–West type robust covariances that grow with h; a bandwidth covering at least the overlap-induced correlation length is a common starting point, not a theorem for every LP.

15.3 LP-IV

If the policy variable x_t is endogenous, estimate y_{t+h}=a_h+\theta_hx_t+\Gamma_h'W_t+\xi_{t+h} by 2SLS with z_t as the instrument for x_t. First stage x_t=\pi z_t+\Lambda'W_t+v_t, second stage with the fitted values. Residualising variables on W_t (denoted \widetilde y,\widetilde x,\widetilde z), with one instrument and one endogenous variable

\theta_h^{IV}=\frac{E(\widetilde z_t\widetilde y_{t+h})}{E(\widetilde z_t\widetilde x_t)}.

The numerator is the instrument's reduced-form effect on the future outcome and the denominator the first stage; dropping the denominator changes the scale and the object estimated. Standard errors must be computed from the IV moment conditions, not read off OLS treating fitted values as raw data. If x_t is the policy rate, the response can be normalised to "the rate rises by one unit on impact", but this is not a controlled intervention that "changes the rate only now and holds the future policy path fixed" — subsequent policy and economic dynamics induced by the instrument are part of the response.

15.4 Asymmetric effects: nest the linear benchmark

Let x_t^+=\max(x_t,0). If the truth is y_t=\beta x_t+u_t but we estimate only y_t=\beta^+x_t^++u_t, we force the effect of negative changes to zero and may create a spurious asymmetry. Estimate

y_t=\alpha+\beta x_t+\delta x_t^++u_t

and test H_0:\delta=0: the slope for negative changes is \beta, for positive \beta+\delta. The same interaction can be put into every horizon's LP (Kilian–Vigfusson on oil prices). Note E(zu)=0 alone does not give E(\max(z,0)u)=0; keeping a function of the instrument exogenous requires independence or sufficient mean restrictions, and relevance must be rechecked. Observing only one-sided narrative shocks also should not be equated with asymmetry between positive and negative effects.

15.5 Level and cumulative responses; state dependence

If y is already a log level, regress the future level y_{t+h}, or use y_{t+h}-y_{t-1} for the cumulative change relative to the pre-shock period; if the left side is a growth rate the coefficient is that period's growth response, not a level response. Summing growth responses to get a level response requires

\operatorname{Var}\Big(\sum_{h=0}^H\widehat\theta_h\Big)=\sum_h\sum_j\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\theta_h,\widehat\theta_j);

standard errors or pointwise bounds must not just be added.

State-dependent LP: let D_{t-1} be a state known before the shock (e.g. a recession indicator),

y_{t+h}=a_h+\theta_h^E(1-D_{t-1})s_t+\theta_h^RD_{t-1}s_t+\Gamma_h'W_t+\xi_{t+h},

and test \theta_h^E=\theta_h^R. Define the state with pre-shock information, otherwise the contemporaneous state may already be affected by the shock; the linear model should be embedded as a testable special case. If s_t is endogenous, the interaction terms also need compatible interacted instruments and rank conditions.

15.6 Practical steps

  1. define the shock, policy variable, outcome and effect unit; state whether the instrument is used directly or as an IV;
  2. choose the maximum horizon H and say whether h is months, quarters or years;
  3. specify pre-shock information and controls, and consider which contemporaneous controls imply timing restrictions or cut off transmission;
  4. construct outcomes, lags and a common/comparable sample for each h (long horizons lose end-of-sample observations);
  5. estimate by OLS or IV with time-series-robust covariances and weak-instrument handling;
  6. plot responses with bands and state the coverage; separate pointwise from path-wide significance;
  7. run sensitivity checks on lags, sample, shock construction and controls.

16. Monetary Policy Shocks: Comparing Six Methods

Intuition. Asking "what is the effect of a rate hike?" can give very different answers under different identification or estimation methods — a difficulty of empirical macro and a rehearsal of the methods of the previous chapters.

16.1 Separate the policy rule from the surprise

A Taylor-type rule: i_t=a_0+a_\pi(\pi_t-\pi^*)+a_y(y_t-y_t^*)+v_t, or using the central bank's forecasts of future inflation and the output gap. The systematic reaction inside the rule differs from the shock v_t outside it. Two historical puzzles: the liquidity puzzle (the short-run relation between some monetary aggregates and interest rates contradicts expectations) and the price puzzle (after a shock identified as tightening, prices rise in the short run; this may involve central-bank information, omitted variables or identification problems).

16.2 Central-bank information and Romer–Romer shocks

The central bank has information the public lacks; controlling for public current output and inflation cannot fully capture policymakers' forecasts, and the residual still contains endogenous reactions to the future. Romer–Romer (2004) use internal Greenbook forecasts and policy records, regress the intended rate change on available information and take the residual as the policy shock, trying to remove the reaction function.

16.3 The six methods compared

"Expansion/contraction" refers to estimated responses under the stated specification, not a universal conclusion.

Method Identification and response construction Reported results and sensitivity
1. CEE-style SVAR block contemporaneous restrictions, VAR-iterated IRF earlier sample (1965m1–1995m6): tightening causes recession; later sample (1983m1–2007m12) may show expansion and a stronger price puzzle
2. R&R hybrid VAR replace the policy series by the R&R residual, keep short-run restrictions original sample contraction; later sample can show expansion; a 100 bp tightening lowers IP by about 2%–3% at a trough around 18 months
3. R&R + LP external shock series, horizon-by-horizon regressions baseline contraction and persistent response; dropping contemporaneous controls or adding factors gives mild expansion and price puzzle
4. R&R Proxy SVAR R&R as external instrument, fewer contemporaneous restrictions plots show expansion, lower unemployment, higher IP, and a price puzzle
5. High-frequency Proxy SVAR high-frequency fed funds futures surprises as instrument; one-year rate etc. in the system tightening lowers IP, raises the one-year rate and excess bond premium; CPI response small in year one
6. High-frequency + LP same information, horizon-by-horizon some reports find IP changes little in year one and then rises, with a more persistent rate and a later price decline; others summarise it as contraction — the literature is not consistent here

The CEE updated specification has industrial production, unemployment, CPI and commodity prices in the first block; the funds rate in the middle; nonborrowed reserves, total reserves and M1 in the last. The R&R-LP baseline controls include the shock, the funds rate, IP, unemployment, CPI and commodity prices with two lags plus several contemporaneous variables — removing the contemporaneous ones changes the implied timing conditions.

16.4 What the comparison teaches

Identification and propagation estimation are two dimensions:

Identifying information VAR-iterated response LP direct response
block / recursive restrictions CEE-style SVAR a comparable LP under matching controls and timing restrictions, but not automatically equivalent
R&R narrative and forecast information hybrid VAR; R&R Proxy SVAR direct R&R shock regression, or R&R as an IV
high-frequency financial surprises high-frequency Proxy SVAR high-frequency LP / LP-IV

A hybrid VAR puts the constructed R&R series in the system and may keep recursive restrictions; a Proxy VAR uses the moment condition between it and the innovations to identify the target column — the same information, but not the same model. Differences in results may come from the shock definition, information set, controls, sample, dynamic restrictions and statistical uncertainty; they should not be blamed on one method being "right" or "wrong". Contemporaneous controls in an LP may imply immediate restrictions similar to recursive identification, or control away part of the transmission.

When a shock named "tightening" is followed by a rise in IP or prices, check in turn: the sign and normalisation of the shock, variable definitions, sample, information set, contemporaneous controls, instrument contamination and statistical bands; only after measurement and identification are clear should a new transmission mechanism be discussed.

17. Maximum Likelihood and the Prediction-Error Decomposition

Intuition. Maximum likelihood asks "for which parameters is the data in front of us least surprising?". Time-series observations are dependent, so marginal densities cannot be multiplied, but the chain rule splits the joint density into a product of "current given past" conditional densities — each of which is the density of a prediction error. This makes the Kalman filter the engine for computing state-space likelihoods.

17.1 Density and likelihood

L(\vartheta;y_{1:T})=p(y_{1:T}\mid\vartheta),\quad\widehat\vartheta=\arg\max_\vartheta\log L,\quad L=p(y_1\mid\vartheta)\prod_{t=2}^Tp(y_t\mid y_{1:t-1},\vartheta).

For continuous data the likelihood is a density value, not the positive probability of "exactly this sample", nor a probability distribution of the parameter given the data. The initial distribution is part of the likelihood; a conditional likelihood can condition on some initial observations, and the convention must be stated. Example (AR(1)): y_1\sim N(c/(1-\phi),\sigma^2/(1-\phi^2)), y_t\mid y_{t-1}\sim N(c+\phi y_{t-1},\sigma^2). The exact likelihood includes the density of y_1; the conditional likelihood fixes y_1 and sums only t\ge2; they differ more in short samples or near a unit root, and at a unit root the stationary initial distribution can no longer be used.

17.2 Conditional normal and the prediction-error decomposition

For jointly normal variables, in the scalar case

E(y\mid x)=\mu_y+\frac{\sigma_{yx}}{\sigma_x^2}(x-\mu_x),\quad\operatorname{Var}(y\mid x)=\sigma_y^2-\frac{\sigma_{yx}^2}{\sigma_x^2};

in the vector case replace the variance ratio by the covariance matrix times an inverse. This underlies the Kalman update. If Y\sim N(\mu,\Omega), \ell=-\frac T2\log2\pi-\frac12\log|\Omega|-\frac12(Y-\mu)'\Omega^{-1}(Y-\mu); working with a T\times T matrix \Omega is costly. Write the positive-definite matrix as \Omega=ADA' (A unit lower triangular, D=\operatorname{diag}(f_1,\ldots,f_T)) and let \eta=A^{-1}(Y-\mu); then \eta_t is the period-by-period prediction innovation and f_t its conditional variance. Hence

\ell(\vartheta)=-\frac12\sum_{t=1}^T\Big[\log(2\pi)+\log f_t+\frac{\eta_t^2}{f_t}\Big].

The likelihood weighs both the size of errors and the uncertainty the model claims: inflating f_t to reduce \eta_t^2/f_t is penalised by \log f_t.

17.3 Parameter constraints and uncertainty

Optimisers search in an unconstrained space \psi and use \vartheta=g(\psi) to impose constraints: positive variance \sigma^2=e^\psi; a (0,1) parameter \theta=1/(1+e^{-\psi}); GARCH: \omega=e^{\psi_0}, \alpha=e^{\psi_1}/D, \beta=e^{\psi_2}/D, D=1+e^{\psi_1}+e^{\psi_2}, guaranteeing \omega>0,\alpha,\beta>0,\alpha+\beta<1. The covariance after the transformation uses the delta method \widehat V_\vartheta=J_g\widehat V_\psi J_g'. Multiple starting points, gradients/curvature, boundaries and convergence diagnostics are part of the optimisation; "the optimiser reports success" does not mean a global optimum or an economically sensible model.

If the optimiser minimises the negative log-likelihood, the inverse Hessian at the optimum approximates the parameter covariance (under correct specification); if the objective is averaged per period, adjust by the sample-size factor; with a Gaussian quasi-likelihood a sandwich covariance is usually needed. Variance parameters near zero create boundary problems, and likelihood-ratio statistics need not follow the usual chi-square approximation.

18. State Space and the Kalman Filter

Intuition. Many important quantities are unseen — a latent trend, a time-varying policy coefficient, the natural rate. A state-space model has two layers: an unseen state that evolves by some law, and observations that are noisy. The Kalman filter answers: with each new observation, how should our belief about the state be updated — like correcting your position with GPS as you walk.

18.1 The model

y_t=H_t\beta_t+Az_t+e_t,\quad e_t\sim N(0,R_t)\qquad\text{(observation equation)}
\beta_t=d+F\beta_{t-1}+v_t,\quad v_t\sim N(0,Q_t)\qquad\text{(state equation)}

\beta_t is the unobserved state, H_t,z_t are known at the relevant time; the basic version assumes the initial state and both noises are jointly Gaussian, serially uncorrelated and mutually orthogonal. Under linearity and Gaussianity the recursion gives exact conditional means and covariances; under weaker conditions it is a linear minimum-mean-square-error estimator but not automatically the full conditional distribution. With a scalar observation H_t is 1\times k; with vector observations it is m\times k.

18.2 Initialisation

Given \beta_{0|0},P_{0|0}. If the state is stationary use the unconditional mean \bar\beta=(I-F)^{-1}d and solve P=FPF'+Q; if the state is a random walk there is no finite stationary unconditional variance, and diffuse initialisation or a prior scale is needed (a large initial uncertainty is common). Initialisation is not a neutral computational choice: it affects early innovations, the likelihood and the state estimates.

18.3 The recursion

Given \beta_{t-1|t-1},P_{t-1|t-1}:

  • Predict the state: \beta_{t|t-1}=d+F\beta_{t-1|t-1}, P_{t|t-1}=FP_{t-1|t-1}F'+Q_t;
  • Predict the observation and compute the innovation: \widehat y_{t|t-1}=H_t\beta_{t|t-1}+Az_t, \eta_t=y_t-\widehat y_{t|t-1}, S_t=H_tP_{t|t-1}H_t'+R_t;
  • Update: K_t=P_{t|t-1}H_t'S_t^{-1}, \beta_{t|t}=\beta_{t|t-1}+K_t\eta_t, P_{t|t}=P_{t|t-1}-K_tH_tP_{t|t-1}.

Numerically, the Joseph form P_{t|t}=(I-K_tH_t)P_{t|t-1}(I-K_tH_t)'+K_tR_tK_t' helps preserve symmetry and positive semi-definiteness; code should solve linear systems rather than form explicit inverses.

Derivation: why this formula. Given past information,

\begin{pmatrix}\beta_t\\y_t\end{pmatrix}\sim N\Big[\begin{pmatrix}a_t\\H_ta_t\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}P_t^-&P_t^-H_t'\\H_tP_t^-&H_tP_t^-H_t'+R_t\end{pmatrix}\Big],

and the conditional-normal formula of 17.2 gives E(\beta_t\mid y_t)=a_t+P_t^-H_t'S_t^{-1}(y_t-H_ta_t), \operatorname{Var}=P_t^--P_t^-H_t'S_t^{-1}H_tP_t^- — exactly the gain and covariance update. (The cross-covariance \operatorname{Cov}(\beta_t,y_t)=P^-H' is k\times m, and its transpose is \operatorname{Cov}(y_t,\beta_t); check dimensions.)

18.4 Intuition and examples

P is the uncertainty about the state, Q the strength of the state's own movement, R the strength of observation noise. With H=1: K_t=P_{t|t-1}/(P_{t|t-1}+R). Prior mean 0, variance 4, R=1, observing y=2: K=0.8, updated mean 1.6, variance 0.8. The noisier the observation, the more cautious the update; the more uncertain the prior, the more the new observation is trusted.

Two successive observations (local-level model y_t=\beta_t+e_t, \beta_t=\beta_{t-1}+v_t, R=1, Q=0.25): after y_1=2, \beta_{1|1}=1.6,P_{1|1}=0.8; predict \beta_{2|1}=1.6, P_{2|1}=0.8+0.25=1.05; observing y_2=1: \eta_2=-0.6, S_2=2.05, K_2=1.05/2.05\approx0.512, \beta_{2|2}\approx1.293, P_{2|2}\approx0.512. The observation pulls the estimate down and lowers uncertainty, but at the next prediction Q injects new state risk, so the filtered covariance need not decrease monotonically.

18.5 Prediction, filtering and smoothing

Object Information used Meaning
\beta_{t\mid t-1} up to t-1 predict the state before seeing the current outcome
\beta_{t\mid t} up to t update after seeing the current outcome
\beta_{t\mid T} full sample smooth ex post using future information

The smoothed curve is more accurate than the real-time filter but was not known at the time. RTS backward smoothing for linear Gaussian models: J_t=P_{t|t}F'P_{t+1|t}^{-1}, \beta_{t|T}=\beta_{t|t}+J_t(\beta_{t+1|T}-\beta_{t+1|t}), P_{t|T}=P_{t|t}+J_t(P_{t+1|T}-P_{t+1|t})J_t'.

18.6 How the Kalman filter sits inside MLE

  1. fix hyperparameters (F,Q,R,d, etc.) and initial conditions;
  2. run the filter for t=1,\ldots,T, obtaining all \eta_t,S_t;
  3. accumulate \ell_t=-\frac12[m\log2\pi+\log|S_t|+\eta_t'S_t^{-1}\eta_t];
  4. the optimiser changes the hyperparameters and repeats until convergence;
  5. rerun the filter at the final hyperparameters to output state paths, variances and forecasts.

The Kalman filter does not itself estimate unknown hyperparameters — "estimate parameters first, then states" means the outer hyperparameter optimisation is completed first.

18.7 Familiar models are state-space models

  • Fixed-coefficient regression: y_t=x_t'\beta+e_t, \beta_t=\beta_{t-1}, Q=0;
  • Time-varying-coefficient regression: y_t=x_t'\beta_t+e_t, \beta_t=\beta_{t-1}+v_t, H_t=x_t';
  • Latent AR(1) with noise: y_t=\beta_t+e_t, \beta_t=\phi\beta_{t-1}+v_t;
  • Local linear trend: y_t=\ell_t+e_t, \begin{pmatrix}\ell_t\\b_t\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\ell_{t-1}\\b_{t-1}\end{pmatrix}+v_t.

The same recursion, different state definitions. Extensions: for linear non-Gaussian models the Kalman filter gives the best linear predictor, not automatically the full conditional expectation; for nonlinear models use the extended Kalman filter (local linearisation, with approximation error); if an observation is missing, only predict and skip the update and likelihood contribution — do not fill with zero and treat it as a real observation.

18.8 Checks after estimation

Standardised innovations \eta_t/\sqrt{S_t}: inspect the mean, ACF, squared ACF and outliers; run sensitivity checks on the initial mean/variance, hyperparameter starting values, boundaries of state-innovation variances and the sample. A smooth or story-friendly state path does not replace these diagnostics; when interpreting policy with real-time data, distinguish the data vintage available then from later revisions; and if the hyperparameters are estimated on the full sample, even a "real-time" historical strategy is not fully implementable.

19. Time-Varying-Parameter Taylor Rules with GARCH

Intuition. A central bank's response to inflation and the output gap may change over time (tougher in a disinflation), and interest-rate adjustment is smoothed. Splitting into two subsamples is too crude to see when changes happen; on the other hand, a sudden volatility in rates may reflect a change in the shock variance rather than in the reaction coefficients — so TVP and GARCH go into the same model.

19.1 The model

Let \pi_t^f,g_t^f be forecasts of future inflation and the output gap available at time t:

r_t=(1-\lambda_t)[b_{0t}+b_{\pi t}\pi_t^f+b_{gt}g_t^f]+\lambda_tr_{t-1}+e_t.

If the original rule uses the inflation gap \pi_t^f-\pi_t^*, then written in levels b_{0t}=b_{0t}^*-b_{\pi t}\pi_t^*, so an intercept that absorbs the unobserved inflation target cannot simply be read as the natural rate. The instantaneous slope in the observation equation is (1-\lambda_t)b_{\pi t}, not b_{\pi t}. The state is the four parameters \beta_t=(b_{0t},b_{\pi t},b_{gt},a_t)':

\beta_t=\beta_{t-1}+v_t,\quad v_t\sim N(0,Q),\ Q=\operatorname{diag}(q_0,q_\pi,q_g,q_a),\quad\lambda_t=\frac1{1+e^{-a_t}}.

Random walks let coefficients change gradually, q_j=0 fixes that coefficient, and the logistic ensures 0<\lambda_t<1. The observation disturbance has variance h_t=\omega+\alpha e_{t-1}^2+\beta h_{t-1}. TVP explains changes in the conditional mean reaction, GARCH changes in the size of conditional noise; ignoring the latter may mistake high volatility for coefficient drift.

19.2 Nonlinearity and linearisation

f_t(\beta)=(1-\lambda(a))(b_0+b_\pi\pi_t^f+b_gg_t^f)+\lambda(a)r_{t-1}

is nonlinear in the state (the logistic multiplies the coefficients). Expand to first order at \bar\beta_t=\beta_{t|t-1}: r_t\approx f_t(\bar\beta_t)+J_t(\beta_t-\bar\beta_t)+e_t. With \bar\lambda=\lambda(\bar a) and \bar m=\bar b_0+\bar b_\pi\pi_t^f+\bar b_gg_t^f:

J_t=\big(1-\bar\lambda,\ (1-\bar\lambda)\pi_t^f,\ (1-\bar\lambda)g_t^f,\ \bar\lambda(1-\bar\lambda)(r_{t-1}-\bar m)\big).

Let y_t^{lin}=r_t-f_t(\bar\beta_t)+J_t\bar\beta_t, giving the approximate linear observation y_t^{lin}\approx J_t\beta_t+e_t (the logistic derivative e^{-a}/(1+e^{-a})^2=\lambda(1-\lambda)). The linearisation point moves with the filtered state, so this is an extended / approximate Kalman method.

Numerical check of the gradient. Take (b_0,b_\pi,b_g,a)=(1,1.5,0.5,0), \lambda=0.5, expected inflation 2, expected gap -1, last rate 4: m=1+3-0.5=3.5, f=0.5\times3.5+0.5\times4=3.75, J=(0.5,1,-0.5,0.125) (0.25\times0.5). If r_{t-1}=\bar m, a small change in the smoothing coefficient has no first-order effect on the rate at that point — which also explains why the smoothing parameter can be hard to identify in some periods.

19.3 Putting the error in the state; latent GARCH

To handle the latent e_t^2, put the error into the state: \widetilde\beta_t=(\beta_t',e_t)', y_t^{lin}=[J_t\ 1]\widetilde\beta_t (observation noise R=0), with state equation \widetilde\beta_t=\mathrm{blockdiag}(I_4,0)\widetilde\beta_{t-1}+\widetilde v_t and \operatorname{Var}(\widetilde v_t\mid\mathcal I_{t-1})=\operatorname{diag}(Q,\widehat h_t); the state is 5-dimensional, and the coefficient output uses the first 4 components and the 4\times4 covariance block. Since e_{t-1} is not directly observed, use E(e_{t-1}^2\mid\mathcal I_{t-1})=[E(e_{t-1}\mid\mathcal I_{t-1})]^2+\operatorname{Var}(e_{t-1}\mid\mathcal I_{t-1}) to update approximately

\widehat h_t=\omega+\alpha\big(\widehat e_{t-1|t-1}^2+P^{ee}_{t-1|t-1}\big)+\beta\widehat h_{t-1}.

If \alpha+\beta<1, h_0=\omega/(1-\alpha-\beta) is the unconditional initial value of the disturbance variance, not the unconditional variance of the random-walk coefficients. Replacing the latent squared shock by its conditional second moment and recursing as Gaussian is an approximation and should not be called an exact integration of the original latent-volatility model.

19.4 Hyperparameters, bands and code

There are typically 7 outer hyperparameters: GARCH \omega,\alpha,\beta and 4 state-innovation variance (or standard-deviation) parameters. Given them, recurse the states, linearise, update variances and the innovation likelihood; after the numerical optimisation converges, run the filter once more to output the four coefficient paths and their variances. The approximate variance of the smoothing coefficient is \operatorname{Var}(\widehat\lambda_t)\approx[\widehat\lambda_t(1-\widehat\lambda_t)]^2\operatorname{Var}(\widehat a_t). Implementations typically impose GARCH constraints with the exponential-normalisation transform; if the state-innovation parameters are squared and then squared again when building the variance, say whether a standard deviation or a variance is reported; and \pm1.65 standard errors correspond to about a 90% band, not 95%.

19.5 Report different uncertainties separately

Uncertainty Source Representation Does it automatically include the others?
state prediction current observation not yet seen and the state moves P_{t\mid t-1} excludes hyperparameter estimation error
state filtering the state is still not directly observed after the observation P_{t\mid t} conditional on given/estimated hyperparameters
observation prediction state uncertainty plus observation noise S_t=HP_{t\mid t-1}H'+R not equal to R
hyperparameter estimation finite-sample estimation of Q,R,F, GARCH parameters Hessian/delta etc. cannot be replaced by the state covariance
nonlinear approximation first-order expansion, latent-variance approximation needs diagnostics not covered by basic Kalman variances

So a plot of \widehat b_{\pi t}\pm1.96\sqrt{P^{\pi\pi}_{t|t}} can only be interpreted as a conditional state band under the stated approximations; it does not cover data revisions, model selection and hyperparameter estimation.

20. Review: Choosing Methods and Easily Confused Concepts

20.1 Routes by research goal

  • Forecasting a single series: fix the transformation, stationarity, seasonality and information set; choose a mean model such as ARMA; adjust dynamics/variance if residuals or squared residuals show structure; evaluate out of sample in time order.
  • Studying long-run relations: check integration orders and deterministic terms, then test for cointegration; if it exists do not discard all level information just to get stationarity — use the error-correction framework to link short-run changes and long-run deviations.
  • Interpreting exogenous policy shocks: define the shock, argue for internal restrictions or external instruments, then choose VAR-iterated or LP direct responses. Standard errors, normalisation and sample differences must be stated along with the identified object.
  • Studying time-varying coefficients: specify what enters the state, how it evolves and how the variance changes; distinguish TVP from volatility changes; estimate by a suitable likelihood and filter, and check initialisation, identification and approximations.

20.2 The most commonly confused concepts

Confused pair The distinction
stationary vs independent stationarity allows time dependence; white noise need not be independent
significant coefficient vs causal significance needs correct inference; causality also needs identification
HAC vs fixing endogeneity HAC only adjusts the covariance; it does not remove bias from correlated regressors
failing to reject a unit root vs proving one failing to reject may reflect a short sample or low power
cointegration vs structural identification a stationary long-run combination does not mean shocks have an economic interpretation
innovations vs structural shocks reduced-form innovations are usually mixtures of several structural shocks
LP vs "assumption-free" LP reduces cross-horizon dynamic restrictions but still relies on shocks/instruments and controls
conditional vs unconditional variance conditional variance can vary while the unconditional variance is constant under second-order stationarity
filtering vs smoothing smoothing uses future observations, so a historical curve is not real-time by default
state covariance vs parameter covariance they refer to different estimation objects and uncertainties
pointwise vs joint forecast bands pointwise bands are not joint coverage of the whole path
"zero now" vs "zero forever" a contemporaneous zero restriction does not make later responses zero
